text: A box-tube arm on two torque servos gives long reach without a motor port.
Build a telescoping box-tube arm on small bearings for a long, stiff reach.
Put a small turret under the intake claw so samples can be picked at any angle without turning the robot.
Use a differential wrist: two servos through bevel gears give pitch and roll, and both share the load.
Put a color sensor in the intake claw so the robot can reject wrong-color samples right away.
Use an Axon Micro for a tiny, light claw at the end of a long arm.
Reuse a proven open-source claw design on your own extension instead of designing one from scratch.
Mix omni corner wheels with center traction wheels for easy turning that resists side pushes.
Mount drive motors inboard and belt-drive each mecanum wheel, so the wheel pods stay narrow and protected.
Single-stage 9t pinion to 108t gear gives 12:1 on bare 6000 rpm motors with no gearbox.
Make wood copies of laser-cut side plates first to test the layout before cutting aluminum.
Use an optical tracking sensor (OTOS) for odometry instead of dead-wheel pods to save space.
Gear fast 1150 rpm drive motors down with a 16T to 42T belt so the robot keeps torque without a new gearbox.
Mount drive wheels on dead axles and belt-drive them so the motors carry no side load.
Mount drive motors in pairs on one plate per side, so each half of the drivetrain comes out as a module.
Steer coaxial swerve modules with Axon Mini servos on belts, so steering uses no motor ports.
Add polycarbonate outer plates over exposed drive gears to keep game pieces and fingers out.
Lay drive motors flat and turn them through miter gears into belts, freeing the space between the side plates.
Stack UltraPlanetary cartridges (4:1 × 5:1) to pick a drive ratio without buying new gearboxes.
A motor-driven tape measure makes a light, long-reach hang.
Drive intakes at both ends of the robot from one motor with long belts along the side.
Use small Rotacaster omni wheels on the intake so game pieces slide in sideways.
Use a 6000 rpm motor directly on the intake for a fast pickup without a gearbox.
A servo-tilted ramp between intake and turret lets the robot hold balls or feed them on demand.
Turn a compliant wheel at each front corner through bevel gears so balls are pulled in from the sides too.
Intakes at the front and back on separate motors let the robot collect while driving either way.
Split the intake into a front compliant-wheel stage and a separately powered middle stage, so balls keep moving into storage.
Turn intake power 90° with a 2:1 bevel set so the motor lies along the side and the roller spans the full width.
Extend a horizontal slide with a side linkage instead of belts or string.
Use IR break-beam sensors in the intake to know the moment a sample is in.
Carry artifacts on a plastic-chain conveyor with small wheels between the intake and the launcher.
Gear the intake pivot servos up (48T to 80T) for more torque when slamming the intake down.
Ten compliant wheels on one long shaft make a cheap full-width intake for 7 cm balls.
Build a clip loader so the robot turns samples into specimens itself.
Use distance sensors on both sides to square up to the wall before scoring specimens.
Deploy a servo brace (floor brake pad or kickstand) so the robot can't be pushed off its aim while shooting.
Lock a drive-powered hang with a ratchet so the robot stays up when power is cut.
Use a servo-shifted PTO in the drivetrain so the drive motors also power the climb.
Swing a gear into mesh on a servo arm to make a simple PTO without a dog clutch.
Add a separate flywheel mass on the shooter shaft so wheel speed drops less between shots.
Drive one flywheel shaft with two motors through 1:1 belts for faster spin-up and recovery.
Belt the counter roller off the flywheel shaft: one motor drives both, their speeds stay locked, and a motor is saved.
Line the counter roller with surgical tubing so it grips the ball without a separate wheel.
Move the hood with a servo through a gear sector so the shot angle can change with distance.
Lift vertical slides with dual-spool winch pulleys so one spool pulls up and the other pulls down.
Use MGN9 linear rails instead of slides for a stiff, compact lift that can't twist.
Mount the horizontal slides inside the drivetrain subassembly so the frame takes the slide loads directly.
Give each storage slot its own servo kicker so balls can be fired in any color order.
Laser distance sensors in storage count balls without depending on color.
Add a separate feeder roller stage between the indexer and the shooter to control when each shot fires.
Put color sensors along the storage ramp to know the order of stored pieces and sort them before the shooter.
A spindexer (rotating three-slot indexer under the shooter) with color sensors lets the robot fire balls in a chosen color order.
An IR break-beam array across the storage counts balls without needing color sensors.
Pair two color sensors per storage slot so artifact color reads reliably wherever the ball sits.
Put color sensors on the turret base looking down into the spindexer slots, so the robot knows each ball's color.
A curved center ramp with one powered wheel lifts balls from the intake to the shooter in a single stage.
Surgical-tubing rollers along an inclined ramp carry balls from the intake up to the turret.
Turn the turret on a large ring gear (205T driven by 60T) for fine aiming resolution from a small actuator.
Build the turret frame from carbon-fiber tubes and printed mounts to keep weight off the turret bearing.
Turn the turret through helical or herringbone gears (e.g. 32T to 160T) for smooth, low-backlash aiming.
Turn the turret with one Axon Max on a 26T pinion to a 120T ring, so the turret uses no motor port.
Route turret wires through a drag-chain ring (inner and outer wiring guides) so the turret turns without a slip ring.
Use a thin-section ring bearing (Kaydon KA060XP0) for the turret; it is flat and leaves the middle open for balls.
Mount the Limelight on the turret so the camera turns with the shooter and stays on the goal.
Belt-drive the turret with a big HTD5 belt around it; the ratio is easy to change and backlash is low.
Gang three servos onto one turret ring gear for a fast, strong turret without using a motor port.
Drive the turret with two servos and read position from an absolute encoder instead of using a motor slot.
